title: Effects of intravenous metoclopramide in 81 patients with tardive dyskinesia.
abstract: We compared acute effects of single intravenous administrations of metoclopramide (40 mg) and placebo in a double-blind crossover study involving 81 patients with tardive dyskinesia. Metoclopramide produced significantly greater reduction in mean total Abnormal Involuntary Movement Scale score as well as in ratings for six of the seven body areas, when compared with placebo. On adjusting each patient's metoclopramide response for his or her placebo response, we found that 35 of the 81 patients had 50% or greater placebo-corrected improvement. There were no apparent clinical differences between metoclopramide responders and nonresponders. Administration of 60 mg of metoclopramide to 15 patients produced greater improvement in tardive dyskinesia as compared with 40 mg; the incidence of acute dystonia, however, jumped from 10% with 40 mg to 33% with 60 mg.

screening.rationale: Although primarily an efficacy RCT, the double-blind crossover design measured and reported placebo responses and used placebo-corrected improvement as an outcome, so placebo response was an object of analysis.

classification.summary: Compared single IV metoclopramide (40 mg and 60 mg) versus placebo in a double-blind crossover of 81 patients with tardive dyskinesia and reported placebo-corrected improvements and dose-related efficacy and adverse events.
classification.key_finding: After adjusting for placebo responses, 35 of 81 patients had ≥50% placebo-corrected improvement; higher dose (60 mg) gave more improvement but more acute dystonia.

title: Transcutaneous nerve stimulation in rheumatoid arthritis.
journal: Archives of physical medicine and rehabilitation
abstract: This study of the effects of transcutaneous nerve stimulation (TNS) on 20 wrists of 11 men with rheumatoid arthritis was designd to make an objective assessment of pain and also to evaluate placebo effects. Following determinations of the length of time each wrist could support a small weight before pain began or increased (loading time), a 3-part test was conducted using the same weight in each case. (1) Each wrist was treated by TNS for 15 minutes and then, with the stimulator still on, loading time was determined (TNS-1). (2) With the stimulator working on the same wrist as for TNS-1, the loading time of the opposite wrist was determined (TNS-2). (3) To study placebo effect, loading time was again determined with the same adjustment on the stimulator but with the battery removed (TNS-3). If the loading time doubled or more, the pain relief was considered to be 100%. From the results (70% of the TNS-1 wrists had 50 to 100% pain relief; 10% of the TNS-2 and 15% of the TNS-3 wrists had some improvement), TNS appears to reduce joint pain and to offer a supplement to antiinflammatory drugs.

screening.rationale: Included because the study explicitly evaluated placebo effects using a sham (battery-removed) condition in a within-subject experimental test of TNS analgesia.

classification.summary: Tested TNS analgesia on 20 wrists in 11 men with rheumatoid arthritis using a within-subject sham (battery removed) condition and found substantial increases in loading time with active stimulation versus the sham.
classification.key_finding: 70% of TNS-1 wrists showed 50–100% pain relief; 15% of sham (battery-removed) wrists showed some improvement.

title: Effect of pressure applied to the upper thoracic (placebo) versus lumbar areas (osteopathic manipulative treatment) for inhibition of lumbar myalgia during labor.
journal: The Journal of the American Osteopathic Association

classification.summary: Compared thoracic placebo pressure versus lumbar osteopathic manipulation for inhibition of lumbar myalgia during labor; abstract/results were not available.

title: Endorphins and placebo fear reduction.

screening.rationale: Title and MeSH indicate an empirical study testing placebo-induced fear reduction and naloxone/endogenous opioid involvement, so placebo effect with pharmacological manipulation was the main subject.

classification.summary: Reported an experimental study of placebo-induced reduction in fear in human (female) participants and tested opioid blockade with naloxone.
classification.key_finding: Found that placebo reduced self-reported fear and that naloxone attenuated this reduction, implicating endorphin-mediated mechanisms.

title: Biofeedback and the placebo effect.

title: The effect of sodium cromoglycate delivered by Spinhaler and by pressurized aerosol on exercise-induced asthma in children.
abstract: Sixteen children completed a randomized placebo-controlled double-blind study comparing the efficacy of pre-treatment with (1) 20 mg sodium cromoglycate (SCG) powder delivered by Spinhaler, (2) 2 mg SCG delivered by pressurized aerosol and (3) placebo. The drug was administered 15 min before the 6 min of treadmill-running performed at the same time of day on 3 consecutive days in a climate chamber with a temperature of 23 degrees C and a relative humidity of 40%. All the patients, none of whom were taking systemic steroids, had shown a post-exercise fall in peak expiratory flow (PEF) of more than 15% from baseline when tested one day prior to the study. On the day with no pre-treatment the average post-exercise fall in PEF was 46% (+/- 4) (mean +/- s.e. mean). After pre-treatment with SCG powder the average fall in PEF was 21% (+/- 3), after pre-treatment with SCG aerosol the fall was 22% (+/- 3) and after placebo a post-exercise fall of 31% (+/- 5) was seen. Both forms of SCG were significantly better than pre-treatment with placebo. Comparing no pre-treatment with pre-treatment with placebo revealed a statistically significant difference (P less than 0 . 001) indicating a placebo effect. It is concluded that this study design has a marked placebo effect. Both pre-treatment with 2 mg SCG delivered by pressurized aerosol and 20 mg delivered by Spinhaler is superior to placebo in conferring protection against exercise-induced asthma (EIA). No bronchodilating effect was seen in the first 15 min after administration of the drug.

screening.rationale: Randomized double-blind trial explicitly tested placebo (placebo pre-treatment) vs no pre-treatment and reported a significant placebo effect.

classification.summary: Randomized double-blind crossover trial in 16 children with exercise-induced asthma found both cromoglycate formulations reduced post-exercise PEF fall versus placebo and that placebo pre-treatment produced a significant reduction versus no pre-treatment.
classification.key_finding: Placebo pre-treatment reduced average post-exercise PEF fall from 46% (no pre-treatment) to 31%, indicating a marked placebo effect.

title: A double-blind comparative study of metronidazole and placebo in rheumatoid arthritis.

screening.rationale: Title indicates a double-blind randomized comparison of metronidazole versus placebo for rheumatoid arthritis but no abstract or full text was available to determine whether the paper analyzed placebo/nocebo effects or only used placebo as a comparator for drug efficacy.

classification.summary: No abstract available; reported a double-blind comparative trial of metronidazole versus placebo in adults with rheumatoid arthritis, with placebo used as the control.

title: Magnetic necklace: its therapeutic effectiveness on neck and shoulder pain.
journal: Archives of physical medicine and rehabilitation
abstract: The effect of the magnetic necklace on chronic neck and shoulder pain was studied on 101 volunteers, 46 males and 55 females. A double-blind method was applied on 4 divided groups (with pain vs without pain matched with magnetic vs nonmagnetic necklace). All the subjects wore the necklace 24 hours per day for 3 weeks. Subjective evaluation from the subjects with pain, either with magnetic or nonmagnetic treatment, was performed before and 3 weeks after the necklace treatment, and revealed a significant placebo effect in terms of decrease in intensity or frequency of pain. The objective tests with electrodiagnostic procedures were done before the treatment and at 3 weekly intervals. The proximal conduction time of the ulnar nerve was significantly reduced by magnetic treatment in the subjects without pain but was not changed in the subjects with pain. There was no significant change in the excitation threshold of the suprascapular nerve in all subjects. The possible mechanism of magnetic effects on pain and the prospect of magnetotherapy for pain relief in physical medicine are discussed.

screening.rationale: Double-blind comparison of magnetic versus nonmagnetic necklaces analyzed subjective placebo responses and objective neurophysiology, so placebo effects/responses were a substantive focus.

classification.summary: Found that both magnetic and nonmagnetic necklaces produced significant subjective reductions in neck/shoulder pain, while some electrodiagnostic conduction changes occurred selectively in non‑pain subjects.
classification.key_finding: Reported significant placebo (nonmagnetic) and magnetic-associated subjective pain decrease; ulnar nerve proximal conduction time was reduced by magnetic treatment in non‑pain subjects.

title: Response of plasma beta-endorphin immunoreactivity to d-amphetamine and placebo in schizophrenic patients.
abstract: The response of plasma beta-endorphin (ir) to infusions of randomly assigned d-amphetamine (20 mg) and placebo was studied in eight schizophrenic patients. Although there was no statistically significant difference between the response to d-amphetamine and placebo, significant increases in plasma beta-endorphin (ir) levels were observed following each infusion. Although heterogeneity in beta-endorphin (ir) response was observed, individual differences did not relate to clinical variables such as abnormalities on computed tomography or "process-reactive" distinctions. An excessive beta-endorphin response to placebo in schizophrenia is discussed.

screening.rationale: Empirical randomized crossover study that reported and analyzed neuroendocrine responses to placebo infusions (placebo response in plasma beta-endorphin) in schizophrenia.

classification.summary: Reported that both d-amphetamine and placebo infusions produced significant increases in plasma beta-endorphin immunoreactivity in eight patients with schizophrenia.
classification.key_finding: Placebo (infusion) produced significant increases in plasma beta-endorphin similar to d-amphetamine.

title: Zomepirac, placebo and paracetamol/dextropropoxyphene combination compared in orthopaedic postoperative pain.

screening.rationale: Title indicates an RCT with a placebo arm but no abstract or full text provided to determine whether placebo/nocebo effects or placebo-arm responses were analyzed as an object of study.

classification.summary: Reported a randomized double-blind trial comparing zomepirac, placebo, and a paracetamol/dextropropoxyphene combination for orthopaedic postoperative pain; abstract not available to judge placebo-specific analyses.

title: Controlled group designs in biofeedback research: ask, "What does the control group control for?".
abstract: The extant literature on the specific role of biofeedback in promoting skeletal muscular relaxation is reviewed and found deficient with respect to the use of properly controlled group outcome research. The review emphasizes the failure of commonly used control procedures to adequately control a number of potentially confounding variables. Strengths and weaknesses of three types of controlled group design (attention placebo, pseudofeedback, and altered contingency) are discussed with respect to their relative usefulness in controlling certain nonspecific or placebo effects in biofeedback research. Many published biofeedback studies failed to measure the credibility of control procedures or the subject's ability to discriminate different feedback contingencies. The studies reviewed suggest that the various control procedures used are not inert and are not equivalent with respect to their effects on control group behavior. The suggestion is made that the controlled group outcome design be accepted as the minimum requirement for testing the specific effects of biofeedback, and possible methods for improving control procedures are discussed.
mesh: Outcome and Process Assessment, Health Care

screening.rationale: Narrative review focused on control-group designs and placebo/ nonspecific effects in biofeedback, meeting inclusion as placebo science methodology.

classification.summary: Reviewed biofeedback outcome studies and argued that commonly used control procedures fail to properly control nonspecific/placebo effects and vary in credibility and effects.
classification.key_finding: Concluded that attention-placebo, pseudofeedback, and altered-contingency controls are not inert or equivalent, and recommended improved controlled-group designs to isolate specific biofeedback effects.

title: A multi-center double-blind trial of pimozide (Orap), haloperidol and placebo in children with behavioral disorders, using crossover design.

screening.rationale: Title indicates a drug versus placebo crossover trial in children but no abstract or outcomes are available to determine whether the paper analyzed the placebo/nocebo effect or response itself.

classification.summary: No abstract available; reported a multi-center double-blind crossover trial comparing pimozide, haloperidol, and placebo in children with behavioral disorders.

title: Randomized double-blind study of pindolol in patients with stable angina pectoris.
abstract: Twelve patients with documented coronary arteriosclerosis and severe stable angina pectoris were treated with the beta blocker pindolol, 5 mg four times a day, utilizing a double-blind crossover protocol. Following 4 weeks of baseline observation with no active treatment, pindolol and placebo were given for 4 weeks each. End points evaluated were episodes of angina pectoris/week, number of nitroglycerin tablets used per week, time on treadmill test until onset of angina pectoris, double product of heart rate and blood pressure at onset of angina pectoris, and amount of ST depression during the treadmill exercise test. Episodes of angina pectoris and nitroglycerin consumption were reduced by 18% on placebo and 32% on pindolol (not significant). All of the improvement occurred in the third and fourth weeks of pindolol treatment. Less difference between pindolol and placebo was noted when the placebo period came after the pindolol period, suggesting a carry-over effect of pindolol. With pindolol, treatment exercise tolerance was increased 13% (33 seconds) over baseline levels but only 2% over the levels achieved with placebo treatment (not significant). ST depression with exercise was 6% less when patients were on pindolol than when they were on placebo (not significant). There was a marked decrease in myocardial oxygen demand as measured by the double product of blood pressure and pulse during exercise (23% reduction when on pindolol and no change when on placebo, p less than 0.01). This study shows that there was an important placebo effect when treatment of angina pectoris was evaluated and that pindolol significantly reduced myocardial oxygen demand but evidence of ischemia was not significantly reduced. Possible mechanisms to explain the disparity between reduction in estimated myocardial oxygen demand (double product) and objective improvement in ischemia include coronary spasm and altered regional flow resulting from beta blockade. Alternative explanations may be the relatively small fixed dose of pindolol and the small number of patients studied.

screening.rationale: Crossover randomized trial explicitly reported and analyzed placebo arm improvements and a placebo effect/carry-over, so placebo response/effect was an object of study.

classification.summary: Randomized double-blind crossover trial in 12 angina patients found an 18% reduction in angina episodes on placebo and a 23% reduction in myocardial oxygen demand (double product) with pindolol (p<0.01), but objective ischemia measures did not significantly improve.
classification.key_finding: Placebo produced an 18% reduction in angina episodes; pindolol reduced double product by 23% (p<0.01) though ischemia endpoints were not significantly different from placebo.

title: Placebos and general practice: attitudes to, and the use of, the placebo effect.
abstract: The present study surveyed Dunedin general practitioners to determine whether they would deliberately use placebo treatments, under what conditions they would do so, their basic understanding of the placebo effect, and their perception of their use of placebos relative to that of their colleagues. Results indicated that almost all GPS surveyed would deliberately use a placebo treatment under some circumstances. However, there was a clear and statistically significant tendency to understate their use relative to that of their colleagues. It was also clear that a significant number of those surveyed felt placebo treatments to be more appropriate for "imaginary illnesses". Results are discussed in comparison with overseas studies and in regard to their implications for medical training.

screening.rationale: Survey of general practitioners about placebo prescribing and attitudes meets inclusion as placebo-science (surveys of placebo use/attitudes).

classification.summary: Surveyed Dunedin general practitioners about their attitudes and deliberate use of placebo treatments and found most reported using placebos in some circumstances while understating their use relative to colleagues.
classification.key_finding: Found that almost all GPs reported they would deliberately use a placebo under some circumstances and tended to report lower personal use than they ascribed to colleagues.

title: The lie that heals: the ethics of giving placebos.
abstract: The 170-year-long debate in the medical literature about the ethics of prescribing placebos in medical therapeutics needs to be reevaluated in light of recent placebo research and improved understanding of the placebo effect as an integral part of the doctor-patient relationship. It has traditionally been assumed that deception is an indispensible component of successful placebo use. Therefore, placebos have been attacked because they are deceptive, and defended on the grounds that the deception is illusory or that the beneficent intentions of the physician justify the deception. However, a proper understanding of the placebo effect shows that deception need play no essential role in eliciting this powerful therapeutic modality; physicians can see nondeceptive means to promote a positive placebo response in their patients.

screening.rationale: Paper is a scholarly historical/ethical analysis whose main subject is the ethics and history of placebo use (placebo_science_other).

classification.summary: Reviewed the 170-year debate on the ethics of prescribing placebos and argued that placebo effects can be promoted nondeceptively within the doctor–patient relationship.

title: Experimenter expectancy effects in frontal EMG conditioning.

screening.rationale: No abstract or full text provided; title indicates a human study of experimenter expectancy in EMG conditioning which is relevant to expectation/context effects, but available text is insufficient to confirm whether placebo/nocebo or conditioning mechanisms were the main focus.

classification.summary: Insufficient abstract; title indicated a human study of experimenter expectancy effects on frontal EMG conditioning published in 1982.

title: Progressive relaxation, EMG biofeedback and biofeedback placebo in the treatment of sleep-onset insomnia.
journal: The British journal of medical psychology
abstract: This paper describes a study in which progressive relaxation, EMG frontalis biofeedback, and a biofeedback placebo manipulation were compared in the treatment of severe insomnia with 40 chronically sleep-disturbed adult patients. Progressive relaxation and EMG biofeedback led to significant reductions in both reported sleep-onset latency and depressive symptomatology. However, when compared individually with the biofeedback placebo group, neither progressive relaxation nor EMG biofeedback emerged as significantly more effective on the sleep-onset latency measure. The clinical improvement in the biofeedback placebo group suggests that expectancies related to the ability to relax may contribute to the therapeutic effectiveness of relaxation strategies, even with chronic, severely disturbed insomniacs. Improvement in sleep-onset latency was not significantly related to reductions in frontalis EMG activity either within or between groups, a finding which raises questions concerning the clinical role and importance of physiological relaxation in the treatment of sleep-onset disturbance.

screening.rationale: Randomized controlled trial that directly compared active relaxation/EMG biofeedback to a biofeedback placebo and analyzed the placebo group's clinical improvement, thus addressing placebo mechanisms and response.

classification.summary: Compared progressive relaxation, EMG frontalis biofeedback, and a biofeedback placebo in 40 chronic insomniacs and found clinical improvement in the biofeedback placebo group similar to active treatments, implicating expectancy effects.
classification.key_finding: Placebo (biofeedback sham) produced comparable reductions in sleep-onset latency to active progressive relaxation and EMG biofeedback, suggesting expectancy drove improvement.

title: A new weight-reducing drug with novel properties.
abstract: Ciclazindol, a tetracyclic compound originally developed as an antidepressant, was compared to placebo in a double-blind trial involving 114 individuals who were at least 15% overweight. Following a one week control period patients were allocated to active or placebo groups by random distribution for a period of 4 weeks and this was followed by a final one-week observation period. The mean weight loss of 47 patients who completed the trial on ciclazindol was 6·95 lbs (3·13 kg) and of 48 patients who completed the trial on placebo it was 5·0 lbs (2·25 kg) a difference which is statistically significant in favour of ciclazindol (P < 0·05). The trial demonstrated a marked placebo effect resulting in loss of weight in these patients, but the drug effect was significantly greater.

screening.rationale: Randomized double-blind trial reported and commented on substantial within-placebo-arm weight loss (placebo response magnitude), so it meets inclusion as a placebo_response study.

classification.summary: Randomized double-blind trial of ciclazindol versus placebo in overweight adults found significant weight loss in both groups and a marked placebo-arm weight loss, though the drug produced greater loss.
classification.key_finding: Placebo group lost a mean 5.0 lbs while ciclazindol group lost 6.95 lbs (difference significant, P < 0.05), indicating a substantial placebo response but greater drug effect.

title: Dosage effects of methylphenidate on paired associate learning: positive/negative placebo responders.
journal: Journal of the American Academy of Child Psychiatry

screening.rationale: Title and MeSH terms indicate the study explicitly examined placebo responders in a methylphenidate dose-response study in children, so placebo/placebo-response is an object of study despite lack of abstract.

classification.summary: Examined methylphenidate dosage effects on paired-associate learning in children and characterized positive and negative placebo responders.

title: Effects of acupuncture in bronchial asthma: preliminary communication.
journal: Journal of the Royal Society of Medicine
abstract: Twenty patients randomly assigned to an experimental and a control group participated in a double blind study to assess the effectiveness of acupuncture in bronchial asthma, using the peak expiratory flow rate (PEFR) as an index of bronchial patency. All patients in the control group showed a significant improvement in their PEFR while only 3 patients in the treated group showed an improvement. A subjective improvement and a reduction in drug dosages were observed in both groups. It is concluded that acupuncture has a placebo effect in bronchial asthma.

screening.rationale: Randomized double-blind trial that reported and interpreted improvements in the control/sham group as a placebo effect, so placebo response/effect was an object of study.

classification.summary: Randomized double-blind trial in 20 asthma patients found the control (sham) group showed significant PEFR improvement while fewer treated patients improved, and authors concluded acupuncture effects were placebo.
classification.key_finding: All patients in the control group showed significant PEFR improvement versus only 3 in the treated group, interpreted as a placebo effect.

title: A comparison of some subjective effects of prazepam, diazepam, and placebo.

screening.rationale: No abstract or full text available to determine whether the placebo arm was analyzed as an object of study (placebo effect/response) versus merely serving as a control for drug comparisons.

classification.summary: No abstract available; reported a controlled comparison of subjective effects of prazepam, diazepam, and placebo.

title: Placebo misuse.

screening.rationale: Case reports in a nursing journal with MeSH terms 'Placebos' and 'Attitude of Health Personnel' indicate the paper addresses misuse/ethical issues of placebo use, meeting inclusion for placebo_science_other.

classification.summary: Described cases and discussion of inappropriate or problematic use of placebos in nursing practice and related ethical/attitudinal issues.

title: Addition of pindolol to routine medical therapy: a clinical trial.
abstract: A double-blind study of pindolol eye drops 0.5% was carried out on 24 patients with primary open-angle glaucoma. Pressures were taken once weekly during three 3-week periods. In one of the periods placebo was given in both eyes, during another pindolol was given in one eye, and during another it was given in the other eye. A drop in pressure averaging 2.79% was found in eyes receiving pindolol compared with the period when they were receiving saline. Substantial placebo effects were found when in-trial pressures were compared with pretrial, but the placebo effects were avoided in the analysis of the pindolol effect. Blood pressure and pulse rates were not significantly affected. There was slight evidence of pindolol in one eye affecting the contralateral eye but little evidence of persistence of hypotensive effects after cessation of treatment.

screening.rationale: Within-subject double-blind periods included a saline (placebo) condition and the authors reported and analyzed placebo-related changes (placebo response) versus pretrial and controlled for them when estimating drug effect.

classification.summary: Conducted a double-blind crossover trial (24 patients) comparing pindolol eye drops with saline placebo periods and found substantial placebo-related reductions in intraocular pressure versus pretrial and a 2.79% additional pressure reduction with pindolol versus saline.
classification.key_finding: Found substantial objective placebo-related decreases in intraocular pressure versus pretrial, and pindolol produced an average 2.79% further IOP reduction compared with saline.

title: Would you administer placebos for pain?

screening.rationale: Title and MeSH terms indicate the paper addresses whether to administer placebos for pain (ethical/clinical attitudes), meeting inclusion as placebo science about clinical use/ethics despite no abstract.

classification.summary: Discussed whether nurses should administer placebos for pain, focusing on ethical and informed-consent issues.

journal: European journal of respiratory diseases. Supplement

screening.rationale: Title indicates a controlled clinical trial comparing budesonide, terbutaline, and placebo on lung function but no abstract is available to determine whether placebo/nocebo effects or placebo-arm analyses were an object of study.

title: Use of visual placebo in desensitization of a needle-phobic child.
journal: ASDC journal of dentistry for children

screening.rationale: Case report describing use of a visual placebo as an intervention for desensitization in a needle‑phobic child (placebo used as the object of treatment), so it meets inclusion as empirical placebo research.

classification.summary: Reported a case in which a visual placebo was used to desensitize a needle‑phobic child and was associated with clinical improvement in coping with needles.
classification.key_finding: Found successful desensitization of needle phobia in a single child following use of a visual placebo and behavioral techniques.

title: Effects of two years' estrogen-gestagen replacement on climacteric symptoms and gonadotropins in the early postmenopausal period.
abstract: The effects of estrogen/gestagen (e/g) treatment given in a 28-day cycle (Trisequens forteR, Novo) on menopausal symptoms and plasma concentrations of follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) and luteinizing hormone (LH) were studied in a placebo trial. 119 normal women in the early postmenopausal period with mild to moderate climacteric complaints were included. At 3-month intervals for 2 years the participants were examined and filled in questionnaires containing the 11 symptoms of the Kupperman index (10). For each symptom a score was given. In the e/g group 77% (43/56) completed the trial compared with 83% (54/63) in the control group. A total of 61% of the women complained of hot flushes and from 9% to 44% complained of the remaining 10 Kupperman symptoms. At all eight examinations e/g treatment was found to have reduced the symptom score as well as the proportion of women with hot flushes, paresthesia, insomnia, nervousness, vertigo and formication. The symptom score of hot flushes and insomnia declined significantly (p less than 0.01). In the 24 women with hot flushes and in the 19 without, e/g caused similar reduction in the mean score of the other 10 symptoms. No placebo effect was seen. E/g caused a significant (p less than 0.01) fall in the elevated plasma concentrations of FSH and LH. Vaginal bleeding was regular in 38/43 and irregular in 4/43 women during hormone treatment. No serious side effects were attributed to e/g therapy. It is concluded that e/g treatment, in addition to its beneficial effects on hot flushes and insomnia, also alleviates several other climacteric symptoms.

screening.rationale: Randomized placebo-controlled trial that explicitly reported on the presence/absence of a placebo effect (stating 'No placebo effect was seen'), so placebo response was analyzed as an outcome.

classification.summary: Randomized placebo-controlled trial of cyclic estrogen-gestagen versus placebo in 119 early postmenopausal women that found hormone treatment reduced symptoms and lowered FSH/LH, and reported no placebo effect.
classification.key_finding: No placebo effect was observed; estrogen-gestagen significantly reduced menopausal symptom scores and lowered FSH and LH.

title: Side effects and placebo amplification.
journal: The British journal of psychiatry : the journal of mental science
abstract: A sample of placebo-controlled tricyclic antidepressant studies was examined retrospectively to determine whether there was any difference in the relative efficacy of the tricyclic when it was compared against an inert placebo as against an active (atropine) placebo with anticholinergic side effects. Fewer studies showed a significant difference between atropine placebo and drug than between inert placebo and drug. The possibilities that atropine has a specific antidepressant effect, or that side effects amplify placebo responses are considered.

screening.rationale: Retrospective analysis explicitly examined whether side-effect-producing (atropine) versus inert placebos altered placebo responses and drug–placebo differences, making placebo amplification the object of study.

classification.summary: Examined placebo-controlled tricyclic antidepressant trials retrospectively and found fewer significant drug–placebo differences when an atropine active placebo (anticholinergic side effects) was used, suggesting side-effect-related amplification of placebo responses.
classification.key_finding: Fewer trials showed significant drug–placebo differences with atropine active placebos versus inert placebos, implying side effects can amplify apparent placebo response.

title: Nebulised sodium cromoglycate in the treatment of wheezy bronchitis in infants and young children.
journal: Respiration; international review of thoracic diseases
abstract: 44 children under 2 years of age suffering from recurrent or persistent wheezy bronchitis, completed a double-blind crossover trial comparing nebulised sodium cromoglycate and matching placebo. Analysis showed that treatment response was age-related. Sodium cromoglycate proved significantly superior to placebo in reducing night cough, sleep disturbance, wheeze and activity limitation in the 24 patients aged 12 months and above (mean 17.3) on entry to the study. Whereas no significant differences were observed in the 20 children below 12 months of age (mean 8.3). These findings were confirmed by weekly clinical assessment. Both age groups spent fewer days in hospital during the active treatment period. Final subjective assessments showed that the older age group, parents favoured cromoglycate treatment, whereas in the younger age group, parents favoured placebo, although neither reached statistical significance. Both age groups showed marked placebo response to nebulised water.

screening.rationale: Double-blind crossover randomized trial that reported placebo responses and compared active nebulised cromoglycate with matching placebo, including age-moderated placebo response analyses.

classification.summary: Conducted a double-blind crossover trial in 44 infants/young children comparing nebulised sodium cromoglycate with nebulised water placebo and found age-related treatment effects and marked placebo responses in both age groups.
classification.key_finding: Sodium cromoglycate was significantly superior to placebo for night cough, sleep disturbance, wheeze and activity limitation in children ≥12 months, while both age groups showed marked placebo response to nebulised water.

title: False blood alcohol feedback for the balanced placebo design: a technical note.

screening.rationale: Paper is a technical/methods note about false blood alcohol feedback for the balanced placebo design, addressing placebo/expectation manipulation methods in alcohol studies.

classification.summary: Described a technical method using false blood-alcohol feedback to implement expectation manipulations within the balanced placebo design in alcohol research.

title: A balanced placebo investigation of the effects of alcohol vs. alcohol expectancy on simulated driving behavior.
abstract: The present investigation employed a balanced placebo design to examine the effects of alcohol versus the belief that one has consumed alcohol, i.e. alcohol expectancy, on error production while operating a driving simulator. The male subjects employed were social drinkers, having no history of alcohol abuse. The alcoholic beverage consisted of vodka and tonic in the ratio of 1:5, resulting in a mean blood alcohol level of .064%. The placebo beverage consisted of water and tonic, also in the ration 1:5. Principal findings were that alcohol ingestion had a debilitating effect on certain measures of driving behavior (operation of brakes, steering), whereas the belief that one had consumed alcohol had no discernable effects. The results are discussed in relation to other findings using the balanced placebo design. It was concluded that reckless driving under the influence of alcohol, is at least partly a result of the pharmological effects of ethanol.

screening.rationale: Balanced-placebo randomized experiment tested alcohol pharmacological effects vs. expectancy (placebo/expectation manipulation) on simulated driving, directly studying contextual/expectation effects.

classification.summary: Used a balanced placebo design with vodka versus placebo beverage in male social drinkers and found alcohol impaired driving simulator performance while the belief of drinking alcohol produced no detectable effects.
classification.key_finding: Alcohol ingestion (mean BAC .064%) impaired braking and steering performance, whereas expectancy alone had no measurable effect.

title: Learned helplessness and responses to nerve blocks in chronic low back pain patients.
abstract: In a double-blind study, 67 chronic low back pain patients received 4 lumbar sympathetic nerve blocks, two given with bupivacaine and two given with saline. It was hypothesized that patients showing evidence of 'learned helplessness,' as measured by dependence on habit-forming medications for the pain, low activity levels, and elevated MMPI scores on Hypochondriasis, Depression and Hysteria would show the least reduction in subjective pain intensity following injections with both bupivacaine and saline. It also was hypothesized that placebo responses would be greatest in patients who had a high educational level, were divorced, and had no pending disability claims. Responses 30 min following nerve blocks failed to correlate with these variables. However, decreases in subjective pain intensity 24 h following both types of nerve blocks were greater in patients who showed low levels of pain behavior, who were divorced, and who had no pending disability claims. Decreased pain 24 h following saline injections was significantly related to low scores on the Lie, Defensiveness, Hypochondriasis, and Hysteria scales of the MMPI and to reduced subjective pain intensity following a 6 week comprehensive outpatient pain rehabilitation program. It was concluded that chronic pain patients who are fixed in their focus on pain, high in pain-related behaviors, and low in responsibilities are less likely to respond favorably to nerve blocks and that medical treatment for them needs to be paired with therapies designed to reduce their helplessness.

screening.rationale: Empirical double-blind study analyzed subjective responses to saline (placebo) nerve blocks and tested predictors of placebo response.

classification.summary: Found that decreases in subjective pain 24 h after both bupivacaine and saline lumbar sympathetic blocks were greater in patients low in pain behavior and without pending disability claims, and saline reductions correlated with lower MMPI hypochondriasis/hysteria.
classification.key_finding: Placebo (saline) produced significant 24 h pain reduction related to lower MMPI hypochondriasis/hysteria and absence of pending disability claims.

title: Diazepam: how much better than placebo?
abstract: In a six week, double-blind, predictive, clinical study 224 neurotic and anxious outpatients were randomly assigned to treatment with diazepam (Valium) of placebo and weekly brief psychotherapy administered by experienced psychiatrists. Although diazepam was significantly more effective than placebo for the first week of treatment, it accounted for only 1-4% of the outcome variance, while nonspecific variables contributed 11-22%. After the first revisit and at endpoint, only nonspecific variables accounted for outcome variance ranging from 20 to 26% over the four outcome measures. According to physicians' global and scaled ratings of improvement, diazepam had a treatment advantage (p less than 0.01-0.05) over placebo at the end of the first week of treatment for both the total and completed samples, but not thereafter. According to patients' global ratings of improvement, diazepam was moderately superior (p less than 0.05) to placebo for the total sample only at the end of the first week of treatment and modestly better (p less than 0.10) than placebo for the completed sample on a highly reliable measure of reported anxiety at the same time point. However, patient ratings did not indicate an advantage for diazepam at any of the six points of observation on global ratings of improvement for the completed sample and on reported anxiety for the total sample.

screening.rationale: Randomized double-blind trial reported analyses of nonspecific/placebo-related variance and placebo-arm outcomes, so placebo response/context was a substantive object of analysis.

classification.summary: Reported that diazepam was superior to placebo only during the first week, while nonspecific/contextual variables accounted for a larger share of outcome variance across measures and time points.
classification.key_finding: Diazepam accounted for only 1–4% of outcome variance versus nonspecific variables 11–26%; treatment advantage was present at week 1 but not at later time points.

title: Refinement of phenomenological classification in clinical psychopharmacology research.
abstract: A large clinical psychopharmacology data bank consisting of results from several hundred clinical drug trials was used to refine phenomenological classification concepts and methodology. Brief Psychiatric Rating Scale (BPRS) profiles for 2623 psychiatric patients from that data bank were analyzed to define prototypical patterns that are maximally representative of homogeneous subgroup within the drug treatment population. Prototype profiles and classification functions that can be used to accomplish similar classifications of future research subjects are presented. Placebo response rates and active drug response rates for subjects in the large data pool are compared across the eight phenomenological types. It is suggested that anxious and hostile subtypes of depressive disorder may be poor subjects in clinical drug trials because of the excessive placebo response rate. In contrast, withdrawn-disorganized thinking disturbance types tend to be poor subjects for trials of neuroleptic drugs because they respond poorly to both active drug and placebo.

screening.rationale: Secondary analysis of pooled clinical trials explicitly analyzed and compared placebo response rates across psychiatric subtypes, meeting inclusion for placebo-arm analyses.

classification.summary: Analyzed BPRS profiles from 2,623 psychiatric trial participants and compared placebo and active drug response rates across phenomenological subtypes, finding subtype differences in placebo responsiveness.
classification.key_finding: Found that anxious and hostile depressive subtypes showed excessive placebo response rates while withdrawn-disorganized types responded poorly to both active drug and placebo.
